html:
The California genocide was the killing of thousands of Native Californians by American settlers, militias and soldiers after the United States took California from Mexico in 1846 to 1848. Together with disease, starvation and forced labour, it cut the Native population from about 150,000 in 1848 to about 30,000 by 1870.

The Native peoples had already been hard hit by the Spanish missions. The Gold Rush of 1848 then brought hundreds of thousands of newcomers who took the rivers, valleys and hunting grounds. Miners and settlers killed Native people with little fear of punishment.

The state took part directly:

  • In 1851 Governor Peter Burnett told the legislature that a war of extermination would continue until the race became extinct.
  • California paid volunteer militias to hunt down Native groups, and the federal government repaid most of the cost.
  • An 1850 law let settlers hold Native people, including children, as bound labourers.

Massacres of whole villages included Bloody Island in 1850 and the killing of the Wiyot on Indian Island in 1860. In Round Valley the Yuki fell from thousands to a few hundred. The Wailaki, Nongatl, Shasta and many others suffered the same. Historians estimate that between about 9,000 and 16,000 Native people were killed outright. In 2019 California's governor formally apologised and called it a genocide.
